messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai grew up in a small coastal town in Vietnam, the only child of a fisherman who drank heavily. Between the ages of six and twelve, her father would come home late, reeking of cheap rice wine, and beat her in her dark bedroom while her mother worked the night shift at a fish-processing plant. She learned to lie perfectly still, listening for the creak of the front gate, her body already tensed before she could hear his footsteps on the stairs. Those nights etched something permanent into her nervous system: the dark became a signal of imminent pain, and the smell of alcohol or the sound of a man’s heavy breathing would make her heart race and her muscles lock.

Now, at twenty-three, Mai is the captain of a small passenger ferry that crosses a river in the Mekong Delta. She is proud of her job—she earned her license at twenty-one, the youngest person in her class—but she has come to realize that her daily life is shaped by invisible constraints she cannot shake. She works only the early-morning and late-afternoon shifts, because the night shift means standing on the bridge in total darkness, which throws her straight back into that childhood terror. Even now, waking in her own cabin at night, she feels her body go rigid, every sense on high alert, and she will lie awake for hours identifying every sound and possible exit. That heightened vigilance spills into her work: she constantly scans the river for hazards, but it also means she is always aware of who is on the bridge with her. She dreads being alone with the male deckhands, especially after sunset. Just the presence of a man she does not know well triggers a surge of negative emotion—fear, sometimes shame—and she finds herself rehearsing escape routes even when there is no danger. She has come to believe the world is fundamentally unsafe, that men in particular are a threat, and that something is fundamentally wrong with her for feeling this way.

The causal loop tightens without her naming it. The more she believes the world is dangerous, the more she scans for threats, and so the more often she notices the triggers that confirm her fear. Her hypervigilance itself—the constant tension, the escape route planning—acts as a lens that magnifies any hint of darkness or male proximity. On the rare occasion she accepts a ride from a male colleague, the entire journey is a crisis: her body is locked, she feels overwhelmed by fear and anger, and afterward she withdraws further, convinced that she is defective because she cannot be a normal person who takes a lift without panic. Her isolation grows. She has stopped visiting her mother’s house, because her mother’s new husband is a man, and being alone with him in the living room at dusk is unbearable. She lies to her mother, claiming she is too busy at work.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a near-collision on the river. A male crew member entered the wheelhouse unexpectedly at twilight, and her reflexive startle caused her to yank the wheel hard, nearly grounding the ferry. The safety officer reported the incident, and Mai was referred to a psychological assessment. She is terrified that she will lose her captain’s license—her only mark of independence—but she is also exhausted by the constant vigilance. What frightens her most is the thought that this is who she is, that the abuse ruined her ability to trust anyone or feel safe anywhere. She hopes, vaguely, that a therapist might finally tell her that she is not broken, that the world is not only darkness and menace, and that she can one night walk into her own cabin without waiting for his footsteps.
